q.young: Did your drink stay down?
q.older: Have you been able to keep a drink down?

candidates.why: Establishes whether fluid the child took actually stayed down, which is the discharge criterion in RCH gastro and RCH vomiting and the nasogastric trigger in NICE 1.3.2.2; decision 3 requires asking what the child managed, not what they drank.

q.young: Can you drink water without throwing up?
q.older: Can you drink something without throwing up?

candidates.why: Same fact reached as a present-tense ability rather than a past outcome, matching NHSGGC's ED rule that the child 'can tolerate oral fluids and do not have ongoing vomiting'.

q.young: Did you throw up after your last drink?
q.older: Did you throw up after the last drink you had?

candidates.why: The same fact with inverted polarity, anchored to one remembered event rather than a stretch of time; NICE separates 'unable to drink it' from 'vomits persistently' and this wording catches the second.

q.young: Are you thirsty?
q.older: Are you feeling thirsty?

candidates.why: The plainest form of the only subjective variable in the three dehydration scales, carried by RCH Dehydration: 'Children with mild dehydration have no clinical signs. They may have increased thirst'.

q.young: Do you want a drink right now?
q.older: Would you like a drink right now?

candidates.why: Reaches thirst through wanting rather than through the word 'thirsty', which a 4-year-old may not own; WHO's own column is 'Thirsty, drinks eagerly' and IMCI asks 'Drinking eagerly, thirsty?'.

q.young: Do you keep wanting drinks?
q.older: Do you keep wanting something to drink?

candidates.why: Asks for a repeated urge rather than a single moment, which is closer to the CDS general-appearance row 'Thirsty, restless' without using an intensity word the screen rejects.

q.young: Have you had a pee since you got here?
q.older: Have you needed a pee since you got here?

candidates.why: Decision 4's preferred form: the raw fact is the child's and the comparison with 'usual' is the nurse's, since the nurse knows the arrival time; sourced from NICE 1.8.1.1 'decreased urine output' and RCH Dehydration.

q.young: Did you go for a pee today?
q.older: Have you been for a pee today?

candidates.why: A day-length window rather than an arrival-anchored one, closer to Gorelick's 'Reduced; not passed in many hours' for a child brought in soon after arriving.

q.young: Do you need a pee right now?
q.older: Do you feel like you need a pee right now?

candidates.why: Asks the present urge instead of a past event, so a child who cannot remember the last time still gives the nurse something; same NICE and RCH Dehydration urine-output line.

q.young: Do bright lights hurt your eyes?
q.older: Do bright lights bother your eyes?

candidates.why: RCH Vomiting's red flag 'Neck stiffness, photophobia and fever in older child'; decision 7 requires the fact already shipped for group head so a child who taps Head and Tummy is asked once.

q.young: Do you want the lights turned off?
q.older: Would you rather the lights were turned down?

candidates.why: Same red flag reached as a preference a child in a lit bay can act on rather than a judgement about their eyes; same shared fact per decision 7.

q.young: Do you throw up when you wake up?
q.older: Have you been throwing up in the morning when you wake up?

candidates.why: RCH Vomiting: 'Early morning vomiting and headache may be due to raised ICP'; asks when in the day it happens, which DURATIONS cannot record because it only records when it started.

q.young: Does throwing up happen in the morning?
q.older: Does the throwing up mostly happen in the morning?

candidates.why: The same raised-ICP line asked as a pattern across days rather than as an event on waking, which is what the guideline sentence actually describes.

q.young: How many times have you thrown up today?
q.older: How many times have you thrown up today?

candidates.why: The packet's own natural wording for the count NICE ('more than twice') and NHSGGC ('three or more times') both threshold; decision 2 requires the count widget so the one reachable boundary is not discarded.

q.young: How many times have you thrown up here?
q.older: How many times have you thrown up since you arrived?

candidates.why: Same MVS and NICE variable over a window the child can see, the same arrival anchor decision 4 chose for item 3, which asks for less aggregation than 'today'.

q.young: How many times have you thrown up this morning?
q.older: How many times have you thrown up since you woke up this morning?

candidates.why: The same count bounded by waking, a landmark a 7-year-old holds better than a clock window; NICE and NHSGGC count over 24 hours and the packet may not say so to the child.

q.young: Is it hard to turn your head?
q.older: Does it feel hard to turn your head?

candidates.why: NICE's 'neck stiffness', NHSGGC's 'Stiff neck' and RCH Vomiting's red flag, turned into something the child discovers by trying rather than a resistance a clinician feels; shares the fact the throat packet ships, per decision 7.

q.young: Can you turn your head to look behind you?
q.older: Can you turn your head to look over your shoulder?

candidates.why: The same three sources framed as a movement the child attempts, which gives a younger child something concrete to do; same shared fact so the child is asked once.

q.young: Has anyone at home thrown up too?
q.older: Has anyone else at home been throwing up too?

candidates.why: The first thing NICE 1.1.1.2 tells a clinician to ask, and the one third of it a child holds; decision 1 requires 'thrown up' here because the natural phrasing uses the banned word.

q.young: Did you see someone else throw up?
q.older: Have you seen anyone else throw up lately?

candidates.why: Decision 10's reason for including this item is that the child reports what they witnessed, so this wording asks exactly that and reaches a classmate as well as a sibling.
